claim: Eukaryotic genomes are compactly packaged inside the cell nucleus by wrapping ~147 bp of DNA around an octamer of histone proteins.
source: Eukaryotic genomes are compactly packaged inside the cell nucleus by wrapping ∼147 bp of DNA around an octamer of histone proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work (Luger et al., 1997; Kornberg, 1977; Onufriev and Schiessel, 2019) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The nucleosome is the chromatin basic repeating unit.
source: This first level of organization establishes the nucleosome, the chromatin basic repeating unit (Luger et al., 1997; Kornberg, 1977; Onufriev and Schiessel, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: CTCF and cohesin execute loop extrusion to form Topologically Associated Domains or TADs.
source: For example, CTCF and cohesin execute loop extrusion to form Topologically Associated Domains or TADs (Rowley and Corces, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rowley and Corces, 2018.

claim: Linker histones bind to the nucleosome at the entry/exit DNA sites to compact chromatin fibers and regulate their architecture.
source: Linker histones (LH) bind to the nucleosome at the entry/exit DNA sites to compact chromatin fibers and regulate their architecture (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022 and Perišić et al., 2019.

claim: Transcription factors bind to regulatory DNA elements, modulating chromatin architecture and accessibility and thereby gene expression.
source: Finally, TFs bind to regulatory DNA elements, modulating chromatin architecture and accessibility and, thereby gene expression (Weidemüller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weidemüller et al., 2021.

claim: Myc is a transcription factor with a C-terminal basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLHZip) motif that has DNA-binding activity and can establish protein-protein interactions.
source: Myc is a TF with a C-terminal basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLHZip) motif that has DNA-binding activity and can establish protein-protein interactions (Meyer and Penn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meyer and Penn, 2008.

claim: Myc regulates a large number of cellular processes, such as proliferation, growth, differentiation and pluripotency, metabolism, and apoptosis.
source: Myc regulates a large number of cellular processes, such as proliferation, growth, differentiation and pluripotency, metabolism, and apoptosis (Eilers and Eisenman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eilers and Eisenman, 2008.

claim: Myc heterodimerizes with Max to form the Myc:Max complex that binds to E-box (5'-CACGTG-3') regulatory DNA elements throughout the genome to control transcription.
source: Myc heterodimerizes with another bHLHZip protein, Max, to form the Myc:Max complex that binds to E-box (5'-CACGTG-3') regulatory DNA elements throughout the genome to control transcription (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991.

claim: Myc:Max heterodimers can form bivalent heterotetramers, allowing them to bring together sequence-distant regions of the genome.
source: Myc:Max heterodimers can further form bivalent heterotetramers, allowing them to bring together sequence-distant regions of the genome (Nair and Burley, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nair and Burley, 2003.

claim: The heterotetramer assembles in a head-to-tail way through the individual leucine zippers of each heterodimer, resulting in the formation of an antiparallel four-helix bundle.
source: The heterotetramer assembles in a head-to-tail way through the individual leucine zippers of each heterodimer, resulting in the formation of an antiparallel four-helix bundle.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the Myc:Max complex.

claim: The interaction between Myc and Max is essential for gene transcriptional repression.
source: This interaction between Myc and Max is essential for gene transcriptional repression (Mao et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2003.

claim: Several Myc-regulated genes contain multiple E-boxes within promoters that are usually separated by 100 bp.
source: Several Myc-regulated genes contain multiple E-boxes within promoters that are usually separated by 100 bp (Coller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coller et al., 2000.

claim: The binding of bivalent Myc:Max to regions with multiple E-boxes can create loops in the chromatin and allow the cooperative regulation at promoters and enhancers containing multiple E-boxes.
source: The binding of bivalent Myc:Max to such regions can create loops in the chromatin and allow the cooperative regulation at promoters and enhancers containing multiple E-boxes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural properties of Myc:Max and the genomic organization of E-boxes.

claim: All-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations have been applied to study the binding of the pioneer TF Oct4 to single nucleosomes.
source: At the nucleosome level, all-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations have been applied to study the binding of the pioneer TF Oct4, alone (Huertas et al., 2020) or with Sox2 (Tan and Takada, 2020), to single nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huertas et al., 2020 and Tan and Takada, 2020.

claim: TF binding has been introduced in polymer models as beads that can reversibly interact with other proteins or with the DNA.
source: At the kb or chromosome level, TF binding has been introduced in polymer models as beads that can reversibly interact with other proteins or with the DNA (Brackley et al., 2013; Buckle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brackley et al., 2013 and Buckle et al., 2018.

claim: The implicit binding of high-mobility group (HMG) proteins to chromatin fibers has been studied at nucleosome resolution.
source: Although the implicit binding of high-mobility group (HMG) proteins to chromatin fibers has been studied at nucleosome resolution (Bajpai et al., 2017), to the best of our knowledge, the effect of TF binding on chromatin architecture has not been studied at nucleosome resolution level.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bajpai et al., 2017.

claim: The effect of TF binding on chromatin architecture has not been studied at nucleosome resolution level prior to this work.
source: Although the implicit binding of high-mobility group (HMG) proteins to chromatin fibers has been studied at nucleosome resolution (Bajpai et al., 2017), to the best of our knowledge, the effect of TF binding on chromatin architecture has not been studied at nucleosome resolution level.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Depending on the linker DNA length, the TF binding position dictates the folding of fibers and the formation of microdomains.
source: Overall, we find that depending on the linker DNA length, the TF binding position dictates the folding of fibers and the formation of microdomains.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 1 and related analyses.

claim: The extent of the effect of TF binding on chromatin compaction and overall shape depends on the presence of LH and histone acetylation, and on the length of linker DNA.
source: The extent of the effect of TF binding on chromatin compaction and overall shape depends on the presence of LH and histone acetylation, and on the length of linker DNA.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 3 and related analyses.

claim: Long linker DNAs and high acetylation levels allow higher TF concentrations to further compact the chromatin fibers.
source: While long linker DNAs and high acetylation levels allow higher TF concentrations to further compact the chromatin fibers, short linkers, and LH impose structural restraints that limit the effect of TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Short linkers and LH impose structural restraints that limit the effect of TF binding.
source: While long linker DNAs and high acetylation levels allow higher TF concentrations to further compact the chromatin fibers, short linkers, and LH impose structural restraints that limit the effect of TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The binding of Myc:Max can repress the expression of the gene Eed by increasing fiber folding and compaction in a way that occludes the promoter region.
source: Finally, we show that the binding of Myc:Max can repress the expression of the gene Eed by increasing fiber folding and compaction in a way that occludes the promoter region; interestingly, this repression can be reversed with high LH density.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The repression of Eed by Myc:Max can be reversed with high LH density.
source: Finally, we show that the binding of Myc:Max can repress the expression of the gene Eed by increasing fiber folding and compaction in a way that occludes the promoter region; interestingly, this repression can be reversed with high LH density.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Contact maps of fibers with medium (44 bp) and long (62 bp) linker DNAs show clear regions of high-frequency contact, or microdomains, as a result of the TF binding, that are dependent on the TF binding positions.
source: Interestingly, contact maps of fibers with both medium (44 bp) (Figure 1A) and long (62 bp) (Figure 1B) linker DNAs show clear regions of high-frequency contact, or microdomains, as a result of the TF binding, that are dependent on the TF binding positions.
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: In fibers with short linkers (26 bp), the formation of microdomains is less clearly identified in the contact maps.
source: In fibers with short linkers (Figure 1C), like 26 bp, the formation of microdomains is less clearly identified in the contact maps.
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 44 and 62 bp linker fibers are less compact and more globular than the 26 bp linker fiber.
source: The 44 and 62 bp linker fibers are less compact and more globular than the 26 bp linker fiber (Perišić et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perišić et al., 2010.

claim: Fibers with 44 and 62 bp linkers are more sensitive to changes in salt concentration and the presence of LH than 26 bp linker fibers.
source: Additionally, these fibers are more sensitive to changes in salt concentration and the presence of LH (Perišić et al., 2010; Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perišić et al., 2010 and Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022.

claim: The presence of more diffuse microdomains in 26 bp fibers can be explained by the rigidity of short-linker fibers in which the linker DNA dictates fiber architecture and produces a highly bent 10 nm ladder-like form with low sensitivity to external and internal parameters.
source: The presence of more diffuse microdomains in 26 bp fibers can be explained by the rigidity of short-linker fibers in which the linker DNA dictates fiber architecture and produces a highly bent 10 nm ladder-like form (Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014) with low sensitivity to external and internal parameters, such as LH binding (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2010; Routh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014; Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2010; and Routh et al., 2008, and inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Longer linker DNAs that give chromatin fibers more flexibility facilitate their folding modulation by TF binding.
source: Thus, longer linker DNAs that give chromatin fibers more flexibility, facilitate their folding modulation by TF binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing differential effects of TF binding on fibers with different linker lengths.

claim: Microdomains emerge in ensemble-based contact maps of life-like fibers similar to the 44 and 62 bp uniform systems.
source: Similar to the 44 and 62 bp uniform systems, microdomains emerge in ensemble-based contact maps of life-like fibers (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Due to the fiber polymorphism triggered by variations in the linker DNA, the microdomains in life-like fibers are slightly more diffuse than in the 44 and 62 bp uniform fibers.
source: Due to the fiber polymorphism triggered by variations in the linker DNA (Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014), the microdomains are slightly more diffuse than in the 44 and 62 bp uniform fibers (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps in Figure 1 and a citation to Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014.

claim: TF binding positions define the organization of life-like chromatin fibers, but the irregularity of the fibers smooths out this effect compared to uniform systems.
source: Thus, TF binding positions define the organization of life-like chromatin fibers, but the irregularity of the fibers smooths out this effect compared to uniform systems; fibers that combine short and long linkers form fluid heterogeneous bent ladders that accommodate TF binding in a more relaxed way than compact 30 nm regular forms.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results comparing life-like and uniform fibers.

claim: Fibers with 44 and 62 bp linkers show clear TF-topology-dependent nucleosome clusters.
source: Fibers with 44 and 62 bp linkers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) show clear TF-topology-dependent nucleosome clusters.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the 26 bp and life-like fibers, the TF dependency of the nucleosome clusters is not as clear.
source: In contrast, for the 26 bp and life-like fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the TF dependency of the nucleosome clusters is not as clear.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microdomains are more diffuse in 26 bp and life-like systems due to fiber rigidity or polymorphism, respectively.
source: These results support the notion that microdomains are more diffuse in these two systems due to fiber rigidity or polymorphism, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering analysis and contact map data.

claim: The contact maps that reveal microdomains are ensemble-based maps in which the contacts from 10 independent trajectories are summed.
source: Importantly, the contact maps that reveal microdomains are ensemble-based maps in which the contacts from 10 independent trajectories are summed.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to generate the contact maps.

claim: Ensemble-based contact maps are analogous to experimental Hi-C maps obtained from a population of cells.
source: These maps are analogous to experimental Hi-C maps obtained from a population of cells.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Hi-C methodology.

claim: The contact maps corresponding to single trajectories, equivalent to single-cell Hi-C maps, do not show a clear formation of microdomains.
source: On the other hand, the contact maps corresponding to single trajectories, equivalent to single-cell Hi-C maps, do not show a clear formation of microdomains.
evidence: This is supported by the single-trajectory contact maps shown in Figure 2.

claim: Checker-board patterns in the ensemble-based map are a product of TF binding not discernible in individual contact maps obtained from single trajectories.
source: As we see from Figure 2 for the 62 bp system with five TF binding regions (Topology 1), checker-board patterns in the ensemble-based map are a product of TF binding not discernible in individual contact maps obtained from single trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of single-trajectory and ensemble-based contact maps in Figure 2.

claim: Cohesin dictates the preferential positioning of boundaries at CTCF sites to produce ensemble TAD structures.
source: These results agree with experimental data showing that cohesin dictates the preferential positioning of boundaries at CTCF sites to produce ensemble TAD structures (Bintu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bintu et al., 2018.

claim: Microdomain structures emerge naturally from tagging of TF binding regions.
source: Here, such microdomain structures emerge naturally from our tagging of TF binding regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Histone acetylation affects chromatin compaction.
source: As we have shown previously, histone acetylation affects chromatin compaction (Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015), size, and compaction of nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021), and can produce the segregation of domains (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015; Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021; and Rao et al., 2017.

claim: Histone acetylation affects the size and compaction of nucleosome clutches.
source: As we have shown previously, histone acetylation affects chromatin compaction (Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015), size, and compaction of nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021), and can produce the segregation of domains (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021.

claim: Histone acetylation can produce the segregation of domains.
source: As we have shown previously, histone acetylation affects chromatin compaction (Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015), size, and compaction of nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021), and can produce the segregation of domains (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rao et al., 2017.

claim: LH density controls chromatin higher-order folding and compaction.
source: Similarly, LH density controls chromatin higher-order folding and compaction (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2019; Grigoryev et al., 2016), and the size and compaction of nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2019; and Grigoryev et al., 2016.

claim: LH density controls the size and compaction of nucleosome clutches.
source: Similarly, LH density controls chromatin higher-order folding and compaction (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Perišić et al., 2019; Grigoryev et al., 2016), and the size and compaction of nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021.

claim: LH binding and tail acetylation act cooperatively to direct fiber folding.
source: In addition, LH binding and tail acetylation act cooperatively to direct fiber folding (Bascom and Schlick, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bascom and Schlick, 2017.

claim: When the linker DNA is short (26 and 35 bp), TF binding does not increase the packing ratio of the fiber.
source: As we see from Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, when the linker DNA is short, such as 26 and 35 bp, TF binding does not increase the packing ratio of the fiber.
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For short linker fibers (26 and 35 bp), the sedimentation coefficient increases significantly from 0 to 25% [TF], and then remains flat.
source: However, the sedimentation coefficient increases significantly from 0 to 25% [TF], and then remains flat.
evidence: This is supported by the sedimentation coefficient data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TF binding saturation occurs at a concentration of 25% for short linker fibers.
source: This indicates that TF binding saturation occurs at a concentration of 25% and that higher TF concentrations do not affect fiber folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the sedimentation coefficient data.

claim: For medium and long linker fibers, both packing ratios and sedimentation coefficients increase upon TF binding.
source: On the other hand, for medium and long linker fibers, both packing ratios and sedimentation coefficients increase upon TF binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The longer the linker DNA, the larger the change in packing ratio upon TF binding at a concentration of 25%.
source: Additionally, the longer the linker DNA, the larger the change in packing ratio upon TF binding at a concentration of 25%.
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TF binding produces a more globular fiber with a higher sedimentation coefficient.
source: Similar to the short linker fibers, TF binding also produces a more globular fiber (Figure 4) with a higher sedimentation coefficient (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the fiber structures in Figure 4 and sedimentation coefficient data in Figure 3A.

claim: For life-like fibers, the effect on packing ratio and sedimentation coefficient is similar to that observed in the medium and long linker uniform fibers.
source: For life-like fibers, the effect on packing ratio and sedimentation coefficient is similar to that observed in the medium and long linker uniform fibers; fibers become more compact and globular upon TF binding (Figure 3A and Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4.

claim: Fluid life-like fibers appear to be less sensitive to the increase of TF concentration than the 44 and 62 bp systems.
source: However, in agreement with the trends observed for the TF binding regions (Figure 1), fluid life-like fibers appear to be less sensitive to the increase of TF concentration than the 44 and 62 bp systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of data for life-like and uniform fibers.

claim: When acetylation islands are incorporated into the chromatin systems, the trends in packing ratios and sedimentation coefficients are similar to wildtype systems, but the extent of the TF binding effect is diminished.
source: When acetylation islands are incorporated into the chromatin systems (Figure 3B), the trends in packing ratios and sedimentation coefficients are similar to wildtype systems, but the extent of the TF binding effect is diminished.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a smaller change in packing ratio when TF binding increases from 0 to 25% in acetylated systems compared to wildtype systems.
source: There is a smaller change in packing ratio when we increase TF binding from 0 to 25%.
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Histone acetylation disrupts internucleosome contacts and opens the chromatin fiber structure.
source: This is because histone acetylation disrupts internucleosome contacts and opens the chromatin fiber structure (Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015), which is opposite to the repressive effect observed by TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015.

claim: When LH is bound to medium and long linker DNA fibers, the effect of TF on chromatin compaction is diminished compared to the wildtype systems.
source: Similarly, when LH is bound to medium and long linker DNA fibers (Figure 3C), the effect of TF on chromatin compaction is diminished compared to the wildtype systems.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LH and TF compete for compacting the chromatin fiber.
source: In this case, LH is a chromatin compactor, like TF binding. Thus, LH and TF compete for compacting the chromatin fiber.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both LH and TF binding compact chromatin.

claim: At 0% TF, the packing ratio of the systems with LH is much higher than the wildtype systems due to LH binding.
source: At 0% TF, the packing ratio of the systems with LH is much higher than the wildtype systems due to LH binding.
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LH binding produces straighter and ordered structures.
source: Moreover, LH binding produces straighter and ordered structures (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022), whereas TF binding produces more globular fibers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022.

claim: TF binding produces more globular fibers.
source: Moreover, LH binding produces straighter and ordered structures (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022), whereas TF binding produces more globular fibers.
evidence: This is supported by the fiber structures shown in Figure 4.

claim: Upon TF binding, fibers with LH are less globular and more straight than the analogous wildtype fibers.
source: Upon TF binding, fibers with LH are less globular and more straight than the analogous wildtype fibers (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the fiber structures shown in Figure 4.

claim: For short linker fibers like 26 and 35 bp with LH, no increase can be observed in the packing ratio upon TF binding.
source: For short linker fibers like 26 and 35 bp, as we saw in the wildtype system, no increase can be observed in the packing ratio upon TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In contrast to the wildtype 26 bp system, TF binding does not increase the sedimentation coefficient when LH is present.
source: In contrast to the wildtype system (Figure 3A), TF binding does not increase the sedimentation coefficient (Figure 3C), and larger standard deviations are obtained, indicating more variability in the fiber structures that create the 1000-structure ensemble.
evidence: This is supported by the sedimentation coefficient data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: With LH, some TF dimer/dimer interactions cannot form in some of the trajectories for the 26 bp system.
source: This is because with LH, some TF dimer/dimer interactions cannot form in some of the trajectories.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TF binding is impaired in the presence of LH for short linker fibers.

claim: LH bound to short linker DNAs produces a fiber rigidity that impairs TF function.
source: Thus, LH bound to short linker DNAs produces a fiber rigidity that impairs TF function.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing impaired TF binding in the presence of LH for short linker fibers.

claim: LH depletion causes excess loading of condensin and topoisomerase II to chromosomes, producing aberrant chromosomes.
source: A similar effect has been seen for condensin and topoisomerase II binding (Choppakatla et al., 2021), where LH depletion causes excess loading of these proteins to chromosomes, producing aberrant chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Choppakatla et al., 2021.

claim: For life-like fibers with LH, the trends in packing ratio and sedimentation appear similar to those of the wildtype systems.
source: Finally, for life-like fibers (Figure 3C), the trends in packing ratio and sedimentation appear similar to those of the wildtype systems (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in packing ratio upon TF binding at a 25% concentration is slightly higher for life-like fibers with LH than for the wildtype system.
source: Interestingly, the increase in packing ratio upon TF binding at a 25% concentration is slightly higher than for the wildtype system (0.85 vs. 0.45 increase).
evidence: This is supported by the packing ratio data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The simultaneous binding of LH and TF to life-like fibers is better accommodated than in uniform fibers.
source: This indicates that the simultaneous binding of LH and TF to life-like fibers is better accommodated than in uniform fibers.
evidence: This is inferred from the packing ratio data.

claim: Fiber fluidity triggered by variations of linker DNA modulates the effect of protein binding on chromatin architecture.
source: Thus, fiber fluidity triggered by variations of linker DNA (Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014) modulates the effect of protein binding on chromatin architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and supported by a citation to Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014.

claim: Myc helps maintain cell pluripotency and inhibits differentiation by activating genes needed for pluripotency and repressing genes that trigger differentiation.
source: Myc helps maintain cell pluripotency and inhibits differentiation by activating genes needed for pluripotency and repressing genes that trigger differentiation (Smith et al., 2010; Krepelova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2010 and Krepelova et al., 2014.

claim: The embryonic ectoderm development gene, Eed, expresses a protein member of the Polycomb-group (PcG) family required for silencing pluripotency genes upon embryonic stem cell (ESC) differentiation.
source: For example, the embryonic ectoderm development gene, Eed, expresses a protein member of the Polycomb-group (PcG) family required for silencing pluripotency genes upon embryonic stem cell (ESC) differentiation (Obier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Obier et al., 2015.

claim: In ESCs, Eed is repressed so that cell differentiation is suppressed.
source: Thus, in ESCs, Eed is repressed so that cell differentiation is suppressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of Eed in silencing pluripotency genes.

claim: TF binding increases the number and frequency of internucleosome contacts in the Eed gene.
source: Figure 5A shows the ensemble-based contact map for the Eed gene with and without TF binding. We see that TF binding increases the number and frequency of internucleosome contacts.
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The density of the contact matrix increases by ~9% upon TF binding in the Eed gene.
source: The density of the matrix increases by ∼9% upon TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the contact map data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TF binding increases hairpin motifs (medium-range contacts) and hierarchical loops (long-range contacts) in the Eed gene.
source: Contact maps obtained from single trajectories (Figure 5B) clearly show that TF binding increases hairpin motifs (medium-range contacts) and hierarchical loops (long-range contacts); these motifs are evident from diagonal and perpendicular regions to the main diagonal of the map (Grigoryev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the single-trajectory contact maps shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Grigoryev et al., 2016.

claim: While short local interactions slightly decrease upon TF binding, local loop interactions increase markedly in the Eed gene.
source: Such an increase in local loop interactions is also observed in the plot of contact frequency versus genomic distance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing that while short local interactions slightly decrease upon TF binding, local loop interactions increase markedly.
evidence: This is supported by the contact frequency plot shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Folding motifs increase fiber compaction in the Eed gene.
source: These folding motifs increase fiber compaction (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the fiber structures shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Upon TF binding, the TF binding regions in the Eed gene are in close proximity, producing a more compact fiber.
source: Fiber configurations show that upon TF binding, the TF binding regions are in close proximity, producing a more compact fiber.
evidence: This is supported by the fiber structures shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The fiber sedimentation coefficient increases upon TF binding in the Eed gene.
source: Furthermore, the fiber sedimentation coefficient increases, while the radius of gyration decreases, upon TF binding (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: The radius of gyration decreases upon TF binding in the Eed gene.
source: Furthermore, the fiber sedimentation coefficient increases, while the radius of gyration decreases, upon TF binding (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: The radii of gyration measurements for the Eed gene agree with experimentally and theoretically determined radii of gyrations for similar size fibers.
source: Such radii of gyration measurements agree with experimentally and theoretically determined radii of gyrations for similar size fibers (Kadam et al., 2023; Boettiger et al., 2016) (e.g. our 62 ± 14 nm Rg is similar to the 43 ± 9 nm Rg predicted for 26 kb regions in Drosophila cells Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kadam et al., 2023 and Boettiger et al., 2016.

claim: The TF binding region 1, which overlaps with the promoter region of Eed, becomes occluded upon TF binding.
source: Significantly, we find that the TF binding region 1, which overlaps with the promoter region, becomes occluded, thus less accessible.
evidence: This is supported by the area and volume measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The area and volume of the promoter region of Eed are reduced ~1.5 times upon TF binding.
source: As reported in Table 1, the area and volume of the promoter region are reduced ∼1.5 times upon TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: Eed mechanism of repression by Myc:Max involves the compaction and occlusion of the promoter region due to increased fiber folding.
source: Thus, Eed mechanism of repression by Myc:Max involves the compaction and occlusion of the promoter region due to increased fiber folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing increased compaction and occlusion of the promoter upon TF binding.

claim: A less accessible promoter will impair gene transcription.
source: A less accessible promoter will impair gene transcription.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of gene regulation.

claim: Upon cell differentiation, LH density increases to ~0.8 LH/nucleosome.
source: Upon cell differentiation, LH density increases to ∼0.8 LH/nucleosome (Woodcock et al., 2006), and Eed needs to be activated so the polycomb protein is expressed and the pluripotency genes are repressed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Woodcock et al., 2006.

claim: Upon cell differentiation, Eed needs to be activated so the polycomb protein is expressed and the pluripotency genes are repressed.
source: Upon cell differentiation, LH density increases to ∼0.8 LH/nucleosome (Woodcock et al., 2006), and Eed needs to be activated so the polycomb protein is expressed and the pluripotency genes are repressed.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the role of Eed in cell differentiation.

claim: When LH density increases to 0.8, the Eed fiber becomes more compact and less flexible due to the repressive effect of LH binding.
source: When ρ increases, the fiber becomes more compact and less flexible (Figure 6 and Table 1) due to the repressive effect of LH binding (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022; Luque et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1, and citations to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022 and Luque et al., 2014.

claim: The change in fiber compaction and flexibility due to increased LH density modulates the impact of TF on the Eed gene.
source: This change in fiber compaction and flexibility modulates the impact of TF.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: The Myc:Max dimers cannot interact when the Eed fiber becomes more rigid and straight due to LH binding at density 0.8.
source: Similar to the effect observed for the 26 bp system in Figure 3, the Myc:Max dimers cannot interact when the fiber becomes more rigid and straight due to LH binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: From the 20 trajectories ran for the Eed system with LH density 0.8 and TF, only one trajectory has dimers engaged.
source: Indeed, from the 20 trajectories ran for this system, only one trajectory has dimers engaged, and thus, the systems with ρ = 0.8 with and without TF exhibit similar properties (Table 1), structures (Figure 6), and genomic contacts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation data.

claim: The Eed systems with LH density 0.8 with and without TF exhibit similar properties, structures, and genomic contacts.
source: Indeed, from the 20 trajectories ran for this system, only one trajectory has dimers engaged, and thus, the systems with ρ = 0.8 with and without TF exhibit similar properties (Table 1), structures (Figure 6), and genomic contacts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 1, Figure 6, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LH is implicated in the activation of genes by impairing the effect of repressive proteins.
source: These results implicate LH in the activation of genes by impairing the effect of repressive proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing that LH impairs TF-mediated repression of Eed.

claim: TF binding creates microdomains that are visible in the ensemble-based contact maps.
source: Our results on different TF binding regions (Figure 1) show that TF binding creates microdomains that are visible in the ensemble-based contact maps; these microdomains are more clearly evident in, and enhanced by longer-linker DNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: Microdomains created by TF binding are more clearly evident in and enhanced by longer-linker DNAs.
source: Our results on different TF binding regions (Figure 1) show that TF binding creates microdomains that are visible in the ensemble-based contact maps; these microdomains are more clearly evident in, and enhanced by longer-linker DNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the contact maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: The clustering of proteins that bridge genomic segments results in TAD-like structures.
source: These results agree with experimental Hi-C maps (Rao et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2018; Hsieh et al., 2020) and polymer modeling studies (Brackley et al., 2013; Brackley et al., 2016; Brackley et al., 2017) showing that the clustering of proteins that bridge genomic segments results in TAD-like structures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and modeling studies.

claim: Silent chromatin has longer linker DNA than active chromatin.
source: Our results showing that fibers with short linkers have more blurred microdomains to geometrical restrictions agree with observations that silent chromatin has longer linker DNA than active chromatin (Valouev et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Valouev et al., 2011.

claim: Longer linkers provide the chromatin fiber with the flexibility needed to fold and create loops that compact the structure and repress transcription.
source: Longer linkers provide the chromatin fiber with the flexibility needed to fold and create loops that compact the structure and repress transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and supported by knowledge of chromatin structure.

claim: Longer linkers and the absence of LH favor the formation of hierarchical loops that compact genes and chromosomes in metaphase chromatin.
source: We showed this for metaphase chromatin where longer linkers and the absence of LH favor the formation of hierarchical loops that compact genes and chromosomes (Grigoryev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grigoryev et al., 2016.

claim: Life-like fibers are sensitive to TF binding positions and form microdomains, although these are less defined than in uniform fibers due to the high plasticity and fluidity of the heterogeneous chromatin.
source: Importantly, life-like fibers, representative of real-life chromatin, are sensitive to TF binding positions and form microdomains, although these are less defined than in uniform fibers due to the high plasticity and fluidity of the heterogeneous chromatin (Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results and a citation to Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014.

claim: Upon TF binding, fibers with short linkers (26 and 35 bp) do not change their packing ratio, whereas fibers with medium and long (44–80 bp) linkers, as well as life-like fibers, become more compact.
source: Similar to the effect on microdomain formation, we also suggest that, upon TF binding, fibers with short linkers (26 and 35 bp) do not change their packing ratio, whereas fibers with medium and long (44–80 bp) linkers, as well as life-like fibers, become more compact (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The role of linker DNA appears to be coupled to the effect that repressive proteins have on the chromatin structure.
source: Thus, the role of linker DNA appears to be coupled to the effect that repressive proteins have on the chromatin structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing differential effects of TF binding on fibers with different linker lengths.

claim: Long linker DNAs produce relaxed DNA trajectories that enable the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally silent heterochromatin regions.
source: This agrees with recent cryo-EM results showing that long linker DNAs produce relaxed DNA trajectories that enable the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally silent heterochromatin regions, whereas short linker DNAs preclude the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally active chromatin (Dombrowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dombrowski et al., 2022.

claim: Short linker DNAs preclude the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally active chromatin.
source: This agrees with recent cryo-EM results showing that long linker DNAs produce relaxed DNA trajectories that enable the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally silent heterochromatin regions, whereas short linker DNAs preclude the binding of LH and produce transcriptionally active chromatin (Dombrowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dombrowski et al., 2022.

claim: Histone tails extend from the nucleosome core and interact with other nucleosomes and with the linker DNA.
source: Histone tails extend from the nucleosome core and interact with other nucleosomes and with the linker DNA (Arya and Schlick, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arya and Schlick, 2006.

claim: When tails are acetylated, they become globular, impairing internucleosome interactions and opening up the chromatin fiber.
source: When tails are acetylated, they become globular, impairing internucleosome interactions and opening up the chromatin fiber (Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collepardo-Guevara et al., 2015.

claim: For fibers with medium, long, and life-like linker DNAs, the effect of TF binding on chromatin compaction is reduced when histone acetylation is introduced.
source: When we introduced histone acetylation, we saw that, for fibers with medium, long, and life-like linker DNAs, the effect of TF binding on chromatin compaction is reduced (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effects of acetylation and TF binding (Myc:Max in particular) on chromatin compaction and architecture are opposite.
source: This is because the effects of acetylation and TF binding (Myc:Max in particular) on chromatin compaction and architecture are opposite.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Histone acetylation can prevent the binding of some pioneer TFs.
source: In line with these results, it has been reported that histone acetylation can prevent the binding of some pioneer TFs (Fuglerud et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuglerud et al., 2018.

claim: Histone acetylation can counter and modulate the repressive effect of proteins that bind to chromatin.
source: Our results thus highlight how histone acetylation can counter and modulate the repressive effect of proteins that bind to chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: LH can impair the effect of TF binding on chromatin architecture.
source: When studying the effect of LH binding, we found that LH can impair the effect of TF binding on chromatin architecture (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fibers with short linkers are particularly affected by LH in terms of TF binding effects.
source: Particularly affected are fibers with short linkers.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The C-terminal domain of LH interacts with the linker DNAs to compact chromatin fibers.
source: The C-terminal domain of LH interacts with the linker DNAs to compact chromatin fibers (Luque et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Luque et al., 2014.

claim: LH competes for the linker DNA with TF binding.
source: Thus, LH competes for the linker DNA with TF binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural roles of LH and TF.

claim: Although LH remains bound to the nucleosome dyad upon TF binding, the C-terminal domain unbinds from the linker DNA.
source: Indeed, recent experiments have shown that although LH remains bound to the nucleosome dyad upon TF binding, the C-terminal domain unbinds from the linker DNA (Burge et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burge et al., 2022.

claim: The LH C-terminal domain influences the regulation of TF binding.
source: These results highlight the influence of the LH C-terminal domain on regulating TF binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results cited.

claim: LH binding produces a rigid and straight fiber that is not flexible enough to be maneuvered by TF binding.
source: LH binding produces a rigid and straight fiber (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022) that is not flexible enough to be maneuvered by TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2022 and inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Although TF and LH binding might not be mutually exclusive as they do not share the same genomic binding sites, LH can indirectly impair TF function by affecting the chromatin fiber architecture.
source: Thus, although TF and LH binding might not be mutually exclusive as they do not share the same genomic binding sites, LH can indirectly impair TF function by affecting the chromatin fiber architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: The effect of LH impairing TF function seems to be less important in life-like fibers.
source: Interestingly, this effect seems to be less important in life-like fibers; these fibers better accommodate simultaneous LH and TF binding.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fiber fluidity appears essential for the regulation of chromatin fibers by multiple protein binding.
source: Thus, fiber fluidity appears essential for the regulation of chromatin fibers by multiple protein binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results comparing life-like and uniform fibers.

claim: TF binding produces the formation of microdomains that can occlude the promoter of Eed, repressing its transcription.
source: Our folding of the Eed gene loci upon repression and activation revealed that TF binding produces the formation of microdomains that can occlude the promoter of Eed, repressing its transcription (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The effect of TF binding occluding the Eed promoter is eliminated by increasing the LH density.
source: However, this effect is eliminated by increasing the LH density (Figure 6), as the fiber flexibility does not allow for the DNA regions with TF bound to come together.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TF and LH binding work together to regulate gene expression.
source: Thus, TF and LH binding work together to regulate gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results on the Eed gene.

claim: The cooperation between TF and LH binding underscores the idea that LH does not always act as a repressor of global transcription.
source: This cooperation further underscores the idea that LH does not always act as a repressor of global transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing LH can counteract TF-mediated repression.

claim: LH depletion can lead to both an increase and a decrease in gene expression in mESC.
source: Furthermore, our emphasis of the LH and TF synergy agrees with results found in mESC showing that LH depletion can lead to both an increase and a decrease in gene expression (Fan et al., 2005), and that LH depletion in Drosophila can down-regulate euchromatin genes (Vujatovic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2005.

claim: LH depletion in Drosophila can down-regulate euchromatin genes.
source: Furthermore, our emphasis of the LH and TF synergy agrees with results found in mESC showing that LH depletion can lead to both an increase and a decrease in gene expression (Fan et al., 2005), and that LH depletion in Drosophila can down-regulate euchromatin genes (Vujatovic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vujatovic et al., 2012.

claim: The epigenetic regulation of chromatin by transcription factors depends on the delicate composition of other internal and external factors present in the cell.
source: As our nucleosome-resolution modeling study at the gene level reveals, the epigenetic regulation of chromatin by transcription factors is a complex dance that depends on the delicate composition of other internal and external factors present in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing interactions between TF, LH, acetylation, and linker DNA length.

claim: TFs collaborate with epigenetic marks and intrinsic chromatin features like linker lengths and nucleosome-free regions to regulate the folding of chromatin at multiple scales and hence gene expression.
source: Thus, TFs collaborate with epigenetic marks and intrinsic chromatin features like linker lengths and nucleosome-free regions to regulate the folding of chromatin at multiple scales and hence gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Microdomains and loops affect access to and topologies of transcription start sites.
source: Because the microdomains and loops affect access to and topologies of transcription start sites, these structural effects translate into effective regulation of cell differentiation and development, as well as human disease progression.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene regulation and inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Structural effects of microdomains and loops translate into effective regulation of cell differentiation and development, as well as human disease progression.
source: Because the microdomains and loops affect access to and topologies of transcription start sites, these structural effects translate into effective regulation of cell differentiation and development, as well as human disease progression.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene regulation and speculative reasoning about broader implications.

claim: Genome regulation in the live cell involves much more than transcription factors, including other chromatin activators and repressors, architectural proteins, and RNAs.
source: Of course, genome regulation in the live cell involves much more than transcription factors. Other chromatin activators and repressors, architectural proteins, and RNAs are also involved.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of genome regulation.

claim: The implicit modeling of TF binding provides clear trends and guiding insights into the regulation of chromatin architecture by protein binding.
source: Although our implicit modeling of TF binding is a simple strategy, it provides clear trends and guiding insights into the regulation of chromatin architecture by protein binding.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of their modeling approach and results.

claim: Further modeling with explicit proteins or consideration of various biomolecules will increase understanding of genome regulation on the many structural and temporal levels involved in complex cellular contexts.
source: Further modeling with explicit proteins or consideration of various biomolecules will undoubtedly increase our understanding of genome regulation on the many structural and temporal levels involved in complex cellular contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.
